claims.event: Native of Maoling who pacified Yuyang, won over the Yingchuan outlaws, was greeted by children on bamboo hobbyhorses in Bing and died aged eighty-six.
Han ruler under whom Guo Ji’s great-great-grandfather was known as a knight-errant.
Father of Guo Ji who served as governor of Shu commandery.
Usurper under whom Guo Ji served in Shanggu and Bing; his chaos left Yuyang lawless.
Ruler whose new regime summoned Guo Ji to Zuo Fengyi and appointed Du Shi to the grand marshal’s staff.
Ruler who appointed Guo Ji to Yong, warned him before Yingchuan and rewarded Du Shi with insignia halberds.
Rebel whose destruction preceded Guo Ji’s transfer to Yuyang.
Mountain outlaw of Yangxia who surrendered to Guo Ji at Yingchuan.
Mountain outlaw of Xiangcheng who surrendered to Guo Ji at Yingchuan.
Rebel holding the north who fled into the Xiongnu when Sui Yu tried to force his surrender to Guo Ji.
General of Lu Fang who plotted to force him to surrender to Guo Ji.
Native of Ji in Henei who killed Xiao Guang, crushed Yang Yi, introduced water-powered bellows in Nanyang and asked to yield his commandery to meritorious officers.
Surrendered rebel in Hedong cut down by Du Shi.
Earlier official to whom contemporaries compared Du Shi.
Ancient founder cited by Du Shi as a ruler who led his people well.
Ancient founder cited by Du Shi as a ruler who led his people well.
Recommended worthy men, memorialized for restoring tiger tallies, and died after being implicated for sending a retainer to avenge his brother.
Man of Qinghe recommended by Du Shi.
Magistrate of Luyang recommended by Du Shi.
Lady whose grievance Du Shi cited in recalling the lord of Xinling’s use of the borrowed tally.
Reported that Du Shi died penniless with no place for burial.
Native of Maoling who studied the Zuo commentary under Liu Xin, kept Guzang without enriching himself, destroyed Wei Mao’s band at the cost of his wife and son, and governed Wudu.
Great-grandfather of Kong Fen who was a palace attendant under Emperor Yuan.
Han ruler under whom Kong Ba served as palace attendant.
Taught Kong Fen the Zuo commentary and praised him to his students.
Usurper whose turmoil drove Kong Fen to Hexi.
General-in-chief of Hexi who appointed Kong Fen to the deliberation bureau and Guzang.
Longxi bandit who killed the Wudu governor and took Kong Fen’s wife and son hostage before being destroyed.
Di headman whom Kong Fen rallied to ambush Wei Mao’s bandits.
Ruler who praised Kong Fen and appointed him to Wudu, and who noticed Zhang Kan before his accession.
Younger brother of Kong Fen who studied in Luoyang and wrote the Excision of the Zuo commentary.
Native of Wan who gave his inheritance to his nephew, urged Wu Han not to retreat from Gongsun Shu, governed Shu honestly and opened rice fields at Hunu in Yuyang.
Ruler in Shu who was lured out and killed beneath the walls of Chengdu.
Grand marshal who on Zhang Kan’s advice did not retreat from Gongsun Shu.
Shu clerk who praised Zhang Kan’s integrity and was made magistrate of Yufu.
Native of Duling who recovered his father’s coffin from a sinking boat, secretly served the jailed Deng Rong, buried his executed teacher Xue Han, and repelled the Xiongnu at Yunzhong with torches.
Zhao general from whom Lian Fan descended, as Emperor Ming recognized.
Great-grandfather of Lian Fan who was general of the right under Emperors Cheng and Ai.
Grandfather of Lian Fan who was grand marshal and Yong department shepherd under Wang Mang.
Usurper under whom Lian Dan served as grand marshal.
Governor of Shu and former subordinate of Lian Dan who twice offered Lian Fan travel funds.
Erudite who taught Lian Fan and was executed in the Prince of Chu case.
Longxi governor who appointed Lian Fan, was impeached and jailed, and was nursed by Fan in disguise.
Prince with whom Xue Han was accused of conspiring.
Han ruler who interrogated and pardoned Lian Fan.
Lifted the Chengdu night-work ban, gave his escort’s horses anonymously to Yan Lin, was criticized for relying on Dou Xian, and was the sworn friend of Qing Hong.
Han ruler at whose funeral at Jingling Lian Fan hurried to mourn.
Lujiang clerk stranded on the road to the imperial mourning who traced and returned Lian Fan’s horses.
Luoyang man who was Lian Fan’s sworn friend and governed Langye and Kuaiji.
Ancient model of friendship paired with Bao Shuya in the saying about Qing Hong and Lian Fan.
Ancient model of friendship paired with Guan Zhong in the saying about Qing Hong and Lian Fan.
Praised in the historian’s judgment, with Lian Fan, for chivalry and integrity before riches.
Han founder cited in the historian’s judgment for summoning Luan Bu.
Man summoned by Gaozu, compared in the historian’s judgment with Lian Fan.
Han ruler cited in the historian’s judgment for drawing in Lian Fan.
Native of Qi in Guanghan who crushed the Qiang in Ba, refused the favors of Wang Sheng and Jiang Jing, delegated to Chen Fan and Ying Si in Runan, and was dismissed through Liang Shang and Yuan Tang.
Han ruler on whose western tour Wang Tang refused improper requests.
Nurse of Emperor An who pressed Wang Tang for favors.
Palace eunuch who pressed Wang Tang for favors and was executed after Emperor An’s death.
Merit clerk to whom Wang Tang entrusted rules and appointments in Runan.
Chief clerk to whom Wang Tang entrusted administration in Runan.
Grand general who resented Wang Tang’s refusal and had him dismissed.
Director of the secretariat who resented Wang Tang’s refusal and had him dismissed.
Shepherd of Yizhou who made Wang Tang’s great-grandson Shang governor of Shu.
Native of Pingling who opened granaries at Wuyuan, prosecuted his old friend the governor of Qinghe as inspector of Ji, and was dismissed in Bing for crushing powerful families.
Han ruler under whom Su Zhang’s ancestor Jian was general of the right.
Grandfather of Su Zhang, a feared and famous critic called a great man, who campaigned with Dou Gu against the northern Xiongnu.
Chariot commandant with whom Su Chun campaigned against the northern Xiongnu and Jushi.
Han ruler under whom Su Zhang passed the examination and Yang Xu’s grandfather served.
Avenged his father Qian by tunnelling into Li Gao’s chamber and desecrating his father’s grave, and was killed with his clan on Duan Jiong’s orders.
Father of Su Buwei who convicted Li Gao and was later tortured to death by him.
Magistrate of Meiyang convicted by Su Qian, who later killed Qian and died of rage after Su Buwei’s revenge.
Palace eunuch whose connections protected Li Gao.
Ancient avenger of his father to whom Su Buwei was compared.
Man of Rencheng who alone likened Su Buwei to Wu Zixu.
Man of Taiyuan who argued that Su Buwei surpassed Wu Zixu.
King of Wu whose power Wu Zixu used to sack Ying.
Grand tutor who summoned Su Buwei in vain.
Man of Hongnong who favored the Su family and fell out with Duan Jiong.
Friend of Li Gao who as colonel of the metropolitan bureau had Su Buwei and his clan killed, and was later executed by Yang Qiu.
Adjutant sent by Duan Jiong to kill Su Buwei, under threat to his father.
Executed Duan Jiong, which was seen as retribution for the Su clan.
Native of Pingyang who was proscribed after Dou Wu’s fall, then as governor of Lujiang routed the Yellow Turbans and Dai Feng.
Han ruler under whom Yang Xu’s father Ru was minister of ceremonies.
Grand general on whose staff Yang Xu served before his fall.
Leader of the Anfeng revolt crushed by Yang Xu.

label.en: Commandery Clerk of the Five Offices

claims.event: Jiangxia soldier who rebelled, killed the Nanyang governor and was killed by Yang Xu and Wang Min.
Toured Nanyang in disguise, killed Zhao Ci, hung up a gift of fish, refused to pay the left outrider fee and so was denied the grand commandancy.
Son of Yang Xu who was shown his father’s meagre possessions and sent home with his mother.
Han ruler who withheld the grand commandancy from Yang Xu, appointed Jia Cong to Jiaozhi and taxed farmland to cast bronze statues.
Native of Liaocheng who pacified mutinous Jiaozhi and stripped the curtains from his carriage as inspector of Ji.
Magistrate of Guanjin who stayed at his post to meet Jia Cong.
Native of Wu who protested Emperor Ling’s land tax, crushed Huang Rang in Lujiang, and held the city against Sun Ce for two years.
Grandfather of Lu Kang with a biography among men of solitary integrity.
Father of Lu Kang who repeatedly refused summons.
Lu ruler whose tax by the mu Lu Kang cited as bringing locust plagues.
Lu ruler whose tax increase Confucius condemned.
Condemned Duke Ai’s tax increase, as cited by Lu Kang.
Lujiang rebel leader crushed by Lu Kang.
Grandson of Lu Kang appointed gentleman of the palace for his grandfather’s victory.
Han ruler whose court rewarded Lu Kang’s tribute.
Warlord at Shouchun who sent Sun Ce to besiege Lu Kang, and whom young Lu Ji visited.
General of Yuan Shu who besieged Lu Kang.
Son of Lu Kang appointed gentleman of the palace for his father’s loyalty.
Youngest son of Lu Kang, famous for hiding oranges when visiting Yuan Shu, later governor of Yulin under Wu.
Praised in the encomium for governing the northern frontier and keeping faith with the children.
Praised in the encomium for governing southern Chu, where the people sang of him.
Praised in the encomium for leaving Guzang in a single carriage without baggage.
Praised in the encomium for leaving Chengdu in a cart with a broken axle.
Praised in the encomium for choosing true friends.
Praised in the encomium for relying on able deputies.
Praised in the encomium, with Jia Cong, as clean and able.
Praised in the encomium, with Yang Xu, as clean and able.
Praised in the encomium for defying Sun Ce until his city fell.
Defied by Lu Kang, according to the encomium.
